tagline: Limestone bluffs and prairie roads cross an older stagecoach trail.
intro: The Smoky Valley Scenic Byway makes a 60-mile horseshoe between WaKeeney and Ogallah, south of I-70. WaKeeney Travel & Tourism highlights changing landscapes, rock outcrops, native grasses and wildflowers along the drive. Here the Smoky Hills mark a transition from mixed-grass prairie to the shortgrass of the Great Plains. Kansas Tourism features the limestone and chalk formations surrounding Cedar Bluff Reservoir among the byway’s attractions. The hills take their name from their hazy blue-gray appearance at sunrise and sunset, a feature highlighted by local tourism.

This modern route crosses the older Smoky Hill Trail. At the end of the Civil War, Butterfield Overland Despatch established service along the trail, carrying goods and travelers between Fort Leavenworth and Denver. Travelers carved names into Threshing Machine Canyon’s walls; two limestone markers identify the byway’s crossings of the old trail. Local builders also used the limestone: Emanuel Lutheran Church’s cornerstone came from Threshing Machine Canyon.

From WaKeeney, take US 283 south toward K-4. Wilcox School stands south of WaKeeney, built from limestone quarried along the Smoky Hill River. Turn east on K-4 toward Brownell, then follow K-147 north beside Cedar Bluff Reservoir and across its dam toward Ogallah. The horseshoe ends back at I-70.

moments.title: Wilcox School
moments.text: Wilcox School’s limestone came from the Smoky Hill River, 1.2 miles south of the building site. Settlers built it in 1886, and it served Wilcox Township for sixty years. The building also hosted church services, literary programs, draft registration and township meetings. After the school closed in 1947, the Hi-Plains Gravel Grinders Motorcycle Club used it as a clubhouse. The one-room schoolhouse survives, with a roof replaced after 2009. It is one of the few remaining rural schoolhouses in Trego County. The school was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006.

moments.title: Cedar Bluff
moments.text: Cedar Bluff’s trees are junipers, misidentified as cedars by early settlers. They cover chalk limestone bluffs on the reservoir’s south side, with a rugged gravel road leading to an overlook above. The water below belongs to a much later project: construction of Cedar Bluff Dam and Reservoir began in 1949 and finished in 1951. Drought in the 1930s had created demand for irrigation and new municipal water supplies. Irrigation use ended in 1978; recreation, flood control and municipal water supply remain its principal uses. The Smoky Hill River flows into the reservoir from the west and out to the east.

moments.title: Threshing Machine Canyon
moments.text: Names carved into Threshing Machine Canyon’s walls record travelers on the old Smoky Hill Trail. The canyon held Bluffton Station on the Butterfield Overland Despatch route. That service carried freight and passengers from Fort Leavenworth to Denver at the end of the Civil War. The carvings date to the mid-19th century. The canyon also supplied stone for Emanuel Lutheran Church, whose congregation laid its cornerstone in 1902. Two limestone markers along the present scenic byway identify crossings of the old trail, keeping the stage route distinct from the modern drive.
